title: GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol
content:
17th November 2026 - Link Blog
GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. OpenAI:
We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work.
They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol. I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models.
6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions.
GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20).
Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra. The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this:
I have a full comparison grid here, but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases:
I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI:
Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data
Here's Sol and here's Astra. Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon.
This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time:
I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting:
https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html  are two videos of the same thing by two different models
I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second
I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned.
Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels
Then later:
OK make it 20s
Here's the exported transcript.
The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example:
When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on.
I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?"

report.summary: OpenAI launches GPT‑6.2 Astra, a cheaper frontier model, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, a low-cost everyday model, as Simon Willison ships LLM 0.38 support and tests both.
report.background: OpenAI has settled into a two-tier release pattern: a frontier model for hard, long-running work and a cheaper model for everyday tasks. The 6.2 generation lands in a crowded field — Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon are the reference points competitors benchmark against. Pricing is the real story: Astra costs 80% of its predecessor, mirroring Fable 5's identical 80% cut, so the two labs are matching each other's discounts almost line for line. Cached input pricing fell even harder, from $1 to $0.40 per million tokens, which matters most for agentic sessions that re-read a large context thousands of times. Simon Willison's quick take covers the usual signals — pricing tables, his pelican drawing test, a three.js coding benchmark, and early community complaints about verbosity.
key_points: Two distinct models ship in one release: gpt-6.2-astra for hard projects and gpt-6.2-sol for everyday work, available immediately in the API and supported by Simon Willison's LLM 0.38 on day one.

Astra drops to $8/$40 per million input/output tokens — 80% of GPT-6 Astra's $10/$50 — exactly matching Claude Fable 5.2's own 80% cut. Cached input falls to $0.40 from $1, a big win for long agentic loops.
Sol stays at $2/$10, the same as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol, and half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol. That means cheaper everyday inference with no price change generation over generation.

Willison's three.js 'Yonkers mech' benchmark was disappointing: neither 6.2 model morphed the city into a mech as convincingly as Claude Fable 5.2 or Gemini 4 Carbon, though Astra composed a side-by-side comparison video from prompts.

Community reaction is mixed. Astra 6.2 trails Fable 5.2 on some benchmarks, and reviewers — notably Theo Browne — complain it interrupts long autonomous runs to ask hyper-specific implementation questions users can't possibly answer.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the headline is price compression at the top end. Frontier capability is getting cheaper faster than it is getting better, and OpenAI and Anthropic are now matching each other's discount ratios almost reflexively — good for buyers, brutal for anyone hoping to compete on margin. For developers, dirt-cheap cached input makes long-horizon agents economically viable: an agent that re-reads a 200k-token context for hours is now a rounding error rather than a budget line. But the reported 'blocked by a question nobody can answer' failure mode is a warning: capability benchmarks are improving more slowly than the ergonomics of supervising autonomous agents. For regular users, the practical effect is cheaper, faster everyday models (Sol unchanged in price) and more agentic products shipping — with the same caveat that these systems still stall in confusing ways.
report.tools: Simon Willison's LLM CLI (v0.38 adds both models) is the quickest way to try them from the terminal; Codex CLI and the Codex desktop app are what he used for the Ultra-effort coding and video-composition tests. For reproducing the benchmark, pair three.js with OpenStreetMap data in a browser, and check Simon's public comparison grid for pelican and pricing side-by-sides against Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon.
